reading.body:
Banking is where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade: Fed SR 11-7 model risk rules already cover credit and AML models, and generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

The pattern is that banking's AI oversight is older than the current generative wave. Credit and AML models have operated under SR 11-7 since 2011, so the sector enters the generative era with pre-existing validation, documentation, and model risk requirements. Treasury's report frames the supervisory conversation, and the Evident AI Banking Index provides a public scoreboard across talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency.

For AI specifically, this means generative deployments in service and compliance inherit a governance burden that most other industries lack. A bank cannot launch a customer-facing chatbot or compliance assistant without treating it as a model under SR 11-7, which slows deployment but also reduces the chance of unmanaged failures. The data does not show scale. It contains no figures on compute demand or power consumption for banking AI, and no adoption rates or model sizes. Governance is the constraint the data documents, not infrastructure.

summary: Fraud detection and credit modelling are decades old; generative AI in service and compliance is the new supervised frontier.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use in finance and insurance, NAICS 52, at 41.0% of firms in the latest period, up from 36.5% in the prior period. The survey first asked the question in September 2023, and the measure is the share of firms answering yes to whether the business used AI in the last two weeks. That is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it covers the whole finance and insurance sector rather than banking alone.

On what the technology is used for, this site's own coverage draws the line at fraud detection and credit models, which it describes as decades old, with generative AI in service and compliance as the new frontier. The same coverage catalogues financial models on this site, tracking the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub with licence, downloads, and release date, refreshed daily, and describes them as models tuned for financial text with tag provenance stated. The catalogue is a view of what is publicly available to build on, not a measure of what banks have deployed.

For where maturity concentrates, this site points to the Evident AI Banking Index from Evident Insights as the benchmark, scoring the major global banks across dozens of quantitative maturity metrics including talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency, and calls it the closest thing banking has to a public AI scoreboard. The material does not report ROI figures, cost savings, or revenue effects from any source, so nothing here supports a claim about returns.

The regulatory posture is the distinctive part. Credit and AML models already operate under the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk management guidance, issued in 2011, and this site's point is that banking is the sector where AI governance predates the AI boom by more than a decade, with the letter listed in the Fed's 2011 supervisory letters index. This site also credits Treasury with mapping the risk surface, describing a Treasury report on AI in financial services, its uses, opportunities, and risks, as framing the US supervisory conversation. The Treasury page cited for that point is a sanctions press release about a gold smuggling and money laundering network, so the AI framing comes from this site's summary rather than from the page text itself.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow reading. Adoption is already substantial and rising in the sector, the public model supply is catalogued and refreshed daily, and the governance expectation is not new: model risk management has applied since 2011, before generative AI was in the picture. The sources here do not quantify returns, do not break adoption down below the sector level, and do not describe specific bank deployments, so a decision has to rest on the measured adoption trend and the existing supervisory framework rather than on any performance evidence in this material.

https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-rel.brief: On International Anti-Corruption Day, Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control sanctioned 28 individuals and businesses tied to a Zimbabwe-based gold smuggling and money-laundering network led by Kamlesh Pattni. The Treasury says the scheme bribed officials, used trusted supporters to conceal ownership, and built a global web of companies to hide illicit activity, depriving Zimbabwe’s citizens of resource benefits while enriching corrupt officials and criminals. Acting Under Secretary Bradley T. Smith noted that “Corruption respects no borders” and that the action demonstrates a whole-of-government approach and collaboration with allies. The Treasury’s move is carried out under Executive Order 13818, which targets serious human-rights abuse and corruption worldwide. International Anti-Corruption Day, observed annually on December 9 since the 2003 UNCAC, aims to raise awareness of anti-corruption initiatives; the United Nations lists 189 parties to the convention.

https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisi.brief: This page lists the Federal Reserve Board of Governors’ 2011 supervision and regulation letters. It notes that a lock icon or https indicates a secure .gov connection and advises “Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.” It also contains guidance on prior notices concerning dividend declarations by savings association subsidiaries of savings and loan holding companies.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/te.brief: The site catalogues what it calls the 1000 most-downloaded open financial models on the Hugging Face Hub, giving each model's licence, download count and release date, with the list refreshed daily. It states that the entries are drawn from the Hugging Face Hub public API, sorted by all-time downloads, and that every model links to its own Hub page. The page records a last-verified date of 2026-09-27.
